speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: It’s not a coincidence that those two events are taking place over three consecutive days. They reflect two different aspects of the same broad set of issues, how best to ensure that the IP system remains fit for purpose in the era of AI with human at the heart of the system and AI used as a tool to empower and support human creativity and innovation, not to replace it. In July at the General Assembly WIPO Director General described WIPO’s work on AI and IP as car with four wheels policy, technical infrastructure, implementation and capacity building. The global forum on Monday and Tuesday were the policy wheel with some moments to reflect on implementation. Today is a technical infrastructure wheel.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: A car is fitting analogy for WIPO’s approach to AI because a car cannot run on one wheel. It needs all four moving in unison. Infrastructure is often the wheel that is treated as an afterthought until something goes wrong, but very important. On the policy side Member States continue to evaluate and make policy choices through their own national and regional processes. As we have heard on Monday from Director General Tan and throughout the discussion at the global forum we may need not only new IP rights but new approaches to the broader administration of IP system.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: As those policy discussions continue and decisions are made, ultimately it will be the role of IP infrastructure to turn those policy choices into practical and operational reality for the participants of the IP ecosystem. Already on the infrastructure side, Generative AI is putting pressure on systems and tools that specific industries need for specific uses. While the policy discussions are playing out, right holders, creators, innovators and AI developers alike all have to find ways to operate now. As the Director General noted on Monday, the path to making the economics of IP in the area of AI work requires workable ways for people to say yes. Because law alone will not solve every problem.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: This is where I triple I comes in, to leverage WIPO’s unique position as a global neutral expert agency that can convene conversations and collaborations and bring those infrastructure issues to the fore. I triple I is not just about copyright. Copyright infrastructure is the best known area of IP infrastructure, although even then it is likely not well known enough. And AI raises infrastructure questions across all of IP. For example, AI is increasingly used as a tool in the innovation process itself.

speaker: ASSISTANT DIRECTOR GENERAL
text: You will hear later a discussion of exactly why and how the notion of AI generated content is playing out in the innovation context and why we cannot just think of copyright. speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: Good morning, everyone. My name is Mateo, and I’m the head of the third-party relationship at Elsevia, a scientific publishing company which is part of the Relax Group. I’m very pleased to present this work developed with colleagues. I was not alone. I would especially like to acknowledge Pascal from Wiley who deserves much of the credit for all this work.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: Together we mapped the scholarly publishing workflow and where AI intersected with it. The aim was to show how industry work, where AI meets their workflow as a starting point for discussing the infrastructure, challenges and opportunities involved. The exercise was valuable to us because it helped us to think through how we look at the topic. By putting the activities together, we could see how closely they depend on one another and how something that happens at one stage can affect what happens much later. The starting point of the workflow is especially clear in scientific publishing and scholarly publishing is not a straight line.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: The published record supports discovery. Discovery informs new research and that research creates new work. So we represented the workflow as a cycle. I’ll use the map to explain how that cycle works, where AI intersects with it and what the exercise helps us to understand. So let’s follow the cycle clockwise starting at the top.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: Yes. Researchers prepare and carry out their work, write it up and submit it to a journal. The journal assesses the submission. If it proceeds, expert editor and reviewer help evaluate it. Accepted work then goes to production and is published.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: The published facilitate this process and subject matter expertise is central, especially in editorial decision and peer review. AI can support tasks such as initial screening, but I will not describe the whole process as machine working while a person simply check it. In many important decisions, the human drives and AI support it. Once published, work needs to be visible. Other researchers need to find it, read it and build on it.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: They may also analyze it computationally or use scientific AI tool slower. That work can then inform new research, bringing us back to the beginning. The circle is simplified by the capture of the basic idea. Science builds on science. Scale is one reason the process needs both system and expertise.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: As one example, Elsevier reported 4.2 million submissions to its 3,000 journal in 2025 with about 800,000 articles published that single year. AI now appears across nearly every stage of this life cycle. It can help people work with information at greater speed and scale, for example, by supporting screening, analysis and discovery. There are real potential benefits. AI can help researchers and editors handle demanding tasks and identify patterns in large collection of information.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: In areas such as medical imaging, for example, it can help flag possible pattern for specialists to examine. But support is not the same as independent judgment. AI tool can miss context or produce information that sounds convincing but is inaccurate or out of date. In science and especially medicine, that matter a lot because people may rely on information to make important decision. So the question is not only what AI can do but also what information it relies on and whether the context around that information remains available.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: That brings me to the infrastructure which has been put at the center of the map. Scholarly publishing has relied on shared infrastructure for many years. At the center of the map are four kinds of infrastructure that support the life cycle, identifiers and metadata, access and entitlement, rights and licensing and integrity and provenance. Scholarly publishing has been the system over many years. Together they help identify works and author, describe access and permitted use, show where content came from and record changes such as correction or attraction.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: AI system may use scholarly content beyond established publishing workflows. They may not always receive or retain all of those signals. For example, a journal may correct or retract the paper after an AI supported system has already used an earlier version. If the update doesn’t reach that system, it may continue to surface the earlier information. The issue is whether correction travel with the content and whether people can trace which version a system relied on.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: That connection between established infrastructure and AI system is one of the things the map helps us to see. The correction example brings us to the loops in the center of the map. They show connection that may not yet be working consistently across the system. The red dashed lines mark pathway the group identified as contested. They highlight places where question around rights and use remain open.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: There are six gaps on the map. I will focus here on 2. G2 which concerns how correction and retraction reach indexes and AI system that may have used an earlier version which we have just seen in the example before. And G3 raises the question of how AI related use can be audited and linked to remuneration where relevant. The circles show how knowledge moves.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: These two gaps show where important connection may need attention. For me, one of the most valuable parts of this work was looking at AI through a system-wide lens. It moved our discussion beyond individual tool and helped us see how the stages depend on one another. The exercise also made clear that scholarly publishing already has substantial infrastructure and expertise. The challenge is ensuring the relevant information travel as content moves through the cycle and into AI system.

speaker: Mr. Matteo Ripamonti
text: I want to acknowledge the value of WIPO creating space for this broad cross-industry view. It helped us better understand the system and gave us a clearer way to discuss where technical collaboration and perhaps other action may be needed. speaker: Ms. Vandana Taxali
text: I just first want to thank WIPO and Garrett and Ryan for the opportunity to present the visual art cycle. So today I’m going to be taking you through the visual art world from the moment an artist conceives a work through exhibition and sale to how an artist is credited and paid and then show you where AI intersects. So at each stage I’ll be showing you what agreements, documents and records identify the artist and ensure that they are paid. It’s these records that also drive value and help prove authenticity and provenance. So I just wanted to share a story.

speaker: Ms. Vandana Taxali
text: So Damien Hurst, an artist, had a work, it was a preserved shark called the physical impossibility of death in the mind of someone living and it was commissioned by Charles Sachi in 1991 for about 50,000 pounds. So in 2004 it reportedly sold to a collector, Steve Cohen, for about 8 to 12 million dollars. So two years before this we had another artist, Eddie Saunders, and he had displayed another preserved shark. Yet when he offered it for a million dollars he received no buyers whatsoever. So why was one worth millions and the other worth nothing?

speaker: Ms. Vandana Taxali
text: Well really this all boils down to the difference was the reputation of the artist, the artwork’s history, scarcity and its recognition in the art market. So even within the art market an original would command more than a limited edition, a limited edition would command more than an open edition. And so this is why records are so essential. They establish an artwork’s creator, identity, history, ownership and rights. They help prove that provenance and authenticity and it makes clear who should be credited and who should be paid.

speaker: Ms. Vandana Taxali
text: So just like my colleague before me, the art life cycle is circular, it’s not linear. Artworks are created, exhibited, sold, collected and licensed often repeatedly and each of these stages generates those records. But those records are often fragmented. So meaning they’re decentralized, they’re stored in different locations and it’s not always easy to piece them together. But now let’s look at each stage of the art life cycle and in the end we’ll look at what happens to these records when AI enters the picture.
